glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Jesus gives the twelve apostles His authority, sends them to the lost sheep of Israel to proclaim and display the kingdom, and prepares them for persecution, fearless confession, divided households, and the cost of loving Him above all, promising that whoever receives them receives Him.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Matthew 10 is the second of Matthew’s five great discourses. Jesus answers the harvest prayer of 9:38 by sending out His own laborers.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Matthew 10:1–4 — Jesus Gives Authority to the Twelve

  • Matthew 10:5–15 — The Twelve Sent to the Lost Sheep of Israel

  • Matthew 10:16–23 — Sheep among Wolves: Persecution and Endurance

  • Matthew 10:24–33 — Do Not Fear Those Who Kill the Body

  • Matthew 10:34–39 — Not Peace but a Sword: Loving Jesus Above All

  • Matthew 10:40–42 — Receiving Jesus’ Messengers

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “He who finds his life will lose it, and he who loses his life for My sake will find it.” (Matthew 10:39)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
The prayer for laborers at the end of chapter 9 is answered at once. Jesus calls the Twelve, names them, and gives them His own authority to heal and to cast out unclean spirits. They are to go first to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (10:6), proclaiming that the kingdom of heaven is at hand. The Davidic King gathers Israel first, and the later commission to all nations (28:19) will widen this mission without abandoning Israel. They travel light and give freely, because they have received freely.

Then Jesus looks beyond this first tour. His messengers will be sheep among wolves, handed over to councils, flogged, and brought before governors and kings. Families will divide over Him. Yet the Spirit of their Father will give them words, the Father who notices a falling sparrow numbers the hairs of their heads, and the One to fear is God, not people. Following Jesus means loving Him above father, mother, son, or daughter and taking up the cross. The chapter ends with comfort: Jesus so identifies with His messengers that even a cup of cold water given to one of them will not lose its reward.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Matthew 10:1–4 — Jesus Gives Authority to the Twelve

Jesus gives the Twelve authority over unclean spirits and every sickness, and Matthew names them, ending with Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Him.

Matthew 10:5–15 — The Twelve Sent to the Lost Sheep of Israel

Jesus sends the Twelve only to the lost sheep of Israel to preach the kingdom, heal, and deliver, giving freely what they have freely received. They are to depend on the hospitality of worthy households and shake off the dust of towns that refuse them.

Matthew 10:16–23 — Sheep among Wolves: Persecution and Endurance

Jesus warns that His messengers will face councils, floggings, rulers, and betrayal within families, but the Spirit of their Father will speak through them. Whoever endures to the end will be saved, and the Son of Man will come before they finish Israel’s cities.

Matthew 10:24–33 — Do Not Fear Those Who Kill the Body

A disciple will be treated as his Master was, but he need not fear people, because God alone has authority over body and soul in hell and the Father watches over every sparrow. Jesus will confess before His Father those who confess Him before others.

Matthew 10:34–39 — Not Peace but a Sword: Loving Jesus Above All

Jesus brings a sword that divides even households. Whoever loves family more than Him or will not take up the cross is not worthy of Him, and losing one’s life for His sake is finding it.

Matthew 10:40–42 — Receiving Jesus’ Messengers

Whoever receives Jesus’ messengers receives Him and the Father who sent Him. Even a cup of cold water given to one of these little ones because he is a disciple will be rewarded.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Matthew 10 shows that the mission of Jesus’ people grows from His compassion and is carried out with His authority. The disciples do not invent the message or the power. They speak the King’s word, do the King’s works, and depend on Him for daily needs.

The chapter also prepares every disciple for opposition. Following Jesus can cost reputation, family peace, and even life, and Jesus says so plainly. Courage does not come from pretending the danger is small. It comes from the Father’s close care, the Spirit’s help in the hour of trial, and the honor of belonging to a King who calls His messengers His own.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Authority shared. Jesus gives His messengers power to heal and deliver (10:1, 8).

Israel first. The Twelve are sent to the lost sheep of Israel (10:5–6).

Endurance under persecution. The Spirit speaks through witnesses who endure to the end (10:19–22).

Fear God, not people. The Father’s care and judgment free disciples to confess Christ (10:28–33).

Christ above all. Love for Jesus outranks every family tie (10:37–39).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Apostles (10:2). Those sent out with authority to represent the one who sends them. Matthew uses the word only here.

Lost sheep of the house of Israel (10:6). Israel’s people, wandering without true shepherds (9:36). The Messiah gathers them first.

Shake off the dust (10:14). A sign that a town that rejected the message is left to answer for its refusal.

The Son of Man comes (10:23). Jesus’ resurrection in royal authority (28:18) is the decisive coming that opens the mission to all nations. His return in glory remains the final horizon.

Take his cross (10:38). To follow Jesus in willing obedience, even when it brings loss, shame, or death.

Little ones (10:42). Jesus’ humble disciples. To welcome them as His disciples is to welcome Him.

focus: Matthew 10 records the second of Jesus’ major discourses as He gives His twelve disciples authority over unclean spirits and sickness and sends them to the lost sheep of the house of Israel to preach that the kingdom of heaven is at hand. His instructions then reach beyond that first journey to the persecution His messengers will face, the Father’s care that frees them from fear, the cost of loving Him above family and life, and the reward of those who receive them.

sections.title: Jesus Gives Authority to the Twelve
sections.summary: Jesus calls His twelve disciples and gives them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal all kinds of sickness and disease. Matthew then lists the names of the twelve apostles, beginning with Simon called Peter and ending with Judas Iscariot, “who also betrayed Him” (Matthew 10:4).

sections.title: The Twelve Sent to the Lost Sheep of Israel
sections.summary: Jesus sends the Twelve not to the Gentiles or Samaritans but to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 10:6), to preach that the kingdom of heaven is at hand and to heal, cleanse, raise the dead, and cast out demons, giving freely as they have received. They are to take no provisions but stay with worthy households, and from any house or city that will not receive them they are to shake off the dust from their feet.

sections.title: Sheep among Wolves: Persecution and Endurance
sections.summary: Jesus sends His disciples as sheep in the midst of wolves and tells them to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves, warning that they will be delivered to councils, scourged, and brought before governors and kings for His sake. When that happens the Spirit of their Father will speak in them, and though they will be hated by all for His name’s sake, “he who endures to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22), and when they are persecuted in one city, they are to flee to another.

sections.title: Do Not Fear Those Who Kill the Body
sections.summary: Since a disciple is not above his teacher, Jesus’ followers should expect the treatment He receives, yet they are not to fear people but to speak openly what He tells them. They are to fear God, who can destroy both soul and body in hell, and to trust the Father who cares for every sparrow, for whoever confesses Jesus before men He will confess before His Father in heaven, and whoever denies Him before men He will deny before His Father.

sections.title: Not Peace but a Sword: Loving Jesus Above All
sections.summary: Jesus declares, “I did not come to bring peace but a sword” (Matthew 10:34), for allegiance to Him will set members of a household against one another. Whoever loves father, mother, son, or daughter more than Him, or does not take up his cross and follow Him, is not worthy of Him, and whoever loses his life for His sake will find it.

sections.title: Receiving Jesus’ Messengers
sections.summary: Jesus declares that whoever receives His messengers receives Him and the One who sent Him. Whoever receives a prophet or a righteous man will receive that one’s reward, and whoever gives one of these little ones a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple will by no means lose his reward.

1.brief: Jesus calls His twelve disciples and gives them power over unclean spirits to cast them out and to heal every kind of sickness and disease. He answers the harvest prayer of chapter 9 by sharing His own authority with those He sends.
1.explain:
“And when He had called His twelve disciples to Him,”

Chapter 9 ended with Jesus telling His disciples to pray for laborers (9:38). Now He answers that prayer by sending some of the ones who prayed. He calls “His twelve disciples” to Himself. The number twelve recalls the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus is gathering a renewed people of God around Himself.

“He gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal all kinds of sickness and all kinds of disease.”

Jesus shares His own authority with them. They will do what He has been doing: cast out “unclean spirits” and heal every kind of sickness. The words echo the summary of His own ministry in 4:23 and 9:35. The disciples go out as His representatives, carrying His authority.
1.notes: The Greek word translated “power” means authority. It is the same word used of Jesus’ authority to forgive sins in 9:6.

2.brief: Matthew lists the twelve apostles, beginning with Simon called Peter and his brother Andrew, and James and John, the sons of Zebedee. These are the first fishermen Jesus called, now named as “apostles,” men sent with His authority.
2.explain:
“Now the names of the twelve apostles are these:”

This is the only place where Matthew calls them “apostles.” The word means those who are sent. They are disciples, learners who follow Jesus, and now apostles, messengers whom He sends.

“first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother;”

“Simon” is named “first.” He is called “Peter,” meaning rock (16:18). He often speaks for the group. His brother “Andrew” was called with him (4:18).

“James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;”

The second pair of brothers are “James” and “John,” the sons of Zebedee. They were fishermen who left their father’s boat to follow Jesus (4:21–22).
2.notes: The lists of the Twelve appear in Matthew 10:2–4, Mark 3:16–19, Luke 6:14–16, and Acts 1:13. Peter is always first and Judas Iscariot always last.

3.brief: The list continues with Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, “Matthew the tax collector,” James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus. Matthew names himself by his former, despised trade, a reminder of the grace that called him.
3.explain:
“Philip and Bartholomew;”

“Philip” was from Bethsaida, the hometown of Peter and Andrew (John 1:44). “Bartholomew” is often identified with Nathanael, whom Philip brought to Jesus (John 1:45).

“Thomas and Matthew the tax collector;”

“Thomas” is remembered for his doubts after the resurrection and for his confession, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). Matthew calls himself “the tax collector.” He does not hide his past. He is a living example of the mercy Jesus showed to sinners (9:9–13).

“James the son of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus;”

This second “James” is identified by his father. “Lebbaeus” was also called “Thaddaeus.” Luke and Acts call him Judas the son of James (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13).
3.notes:
Only Matthew’s list adds the tax collector to Matthew’s name.

Some manuscripts read only Thaddaeus in this verse.

4.brief: The list ends with Simon the Cananite and “Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed Him.” From the beginning Matthew marks the betrayer within the chosen circle.
4.explain:
“Simon the Cananite,”

This “Simon” is distinguished from Simon Peter. “Cananite” comes from an Aramaic word meaning zealous. Luke calls him Simon the Zealot (Luke 6:15). He may once have belonged to a movement that zealously opposed Roman rule.

Jesus’ chosen twelve included a tax collector who had worked with Rome and a zealot who may have opposed it. Jesus brings together people who would otherwise have been enemies.

“and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed Him.”

The list ends with “Judas Iscariot.” Matthew identifies him by what he will do: he “betrayed Him.” Even Judas received authority and was sent out with the others.
4.notes: Iscariot may mean man of Kerioth, a town in southern Judea (Joshua 15:25). If so, Judas may have been the only one of the Twelve from Judea.

5.brief: Jesus sends out the Twelve with instructions not to go among the Gentiles or enter a Samaritan town. This first mission has a deliberately limited scope.
5.explain:
“These twelve Jesus sent out and commanded them, saying:”

Jesus sends out the Twelve with instructions. The rest of the chapter records what He told them.

“Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans.”

For this mission, Jesus limits where they may go. They must not go to “the Gentiles,” non-Jewish peoples. They must not enter “a city of the Samaritans,” the mixed people living between Galilee and Judea.

This restriction belongs to this particular sending. It does not mean Jesus cares nothing for the nations. After His resurrection, He will send His disciples to all nations (28:19).
5.notes: The Samaritans descended from Israelites who remained in the northern kingdom and from peoples the Assyrians settled there (2 Kings 17:24–41). Jews and Samaritans had long been divided.

6.brief: Jesus sends the Twelve instead “to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” As Israel’s promised King, Jesus seeks His own people first, a priority later widened to all nations without abandoning Israel.
6.explain:
“But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

The disciples are to go to Israel first. Jesus describes the people as “lost sheep.” He had seen them as sheep without a shepherd (9:36).

The Messiah came first to the people God had promised to save. God made His promises to Abraham and his descendants. Jesus keeps those promises by gathering Israel first. Later the mission will reach the nations, and the blessing promised to Abraham will reach all the families of the earth (Genesis 22:18). Israel is not replaced. The King’s people grow around Him to include the nations.
6.notes:
Jesus says the same of His own mission in 15:24: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

Paul writes that Christ became a servant to the circumcision to confirm the promises made to the fathers, and that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy (Romans 15:8–9).

7.brief: As the Twelve go, they are to preach, “The kingdom of heaven is at hand.” They carry the same message Jesus Himself proclaims.
7.explain:
“And as you go, preach, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand.”

The disciples carry the same message that John and Jesus preached (3:2; 4:17). God’s rule has come near in the person of Jesus.
7.notes: Matthew uses the phrase kingdom of heaven where Mark and Luke usually say kingdom of God. Jews often spoke of heaven out of reverence for God’s name.

8.brief: The Twelve are to heal the sick, cleanse lepers, raise the dead, and cast out demons, and “Freely you have received, freely give.” Their works display the kingdom’s restoring power, and since they received this authority as a gift, they must not sell it.
8.explain:
“Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out demons.”

The disciples are to do the works Jesus has been doing in chapters 8–9. He has healed the sick, cleansed a leper, raised the dead, and cast out demons. Their deeds will show that God’s kingdom has come.

“Freely you have received, freely give.”

The disciples received their authority as a free gift. They must not sell it. They are to give freely what grace has given them.
8.notes:
Some manuscripts do not include raise the dead.

Peter refused money from Simon the sorcerer, who wanted to buy the power to give the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:18–20).

9.brief: Jesus tells the Twelve to take no gold, silver, or copper in their money belts. Their mission depends on God’s provision, not their own resources.
9.explain:
“Provide neither gold nor silver nor copper in your money belts,”

Jesus tells them not to take money. A money belt was a sash or girdle where coins were often carried. They are not to provide for themselves in advance.
9.notes: The Greek word translated “provide” can mean to acquire or get. Some read it as a command not to earn money from their ministry.

10.brief: Nor are Jesus’ messengers to take a travel bag, an extra tunic, sandals, or staffs, because “a worker is worthy of his food.” They are to travel light and trust God to supply their needs through those who receive them.
10.explain:
“nor bag for your journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor staffs;”

They are not to take a traveler’s “bag” for supplies, an extra tunic, spare sandals, or a staff. They travel light. They depend on God and on the people who welcome them.

These instructions belong to this particular sending. Later Jesus will tell His disciples to take a money bag and a sack (Luke 22:35–36). What remains for every disciple is the principle of dependence on God and generosity in ministry.

“for a worker is worthy of his food.”

God will provide for them through the hospitality of others. A “worker” deserves to be fed.
10.notes:
Mark 6:8–9 allows a staff and sandals. Matthew’s wording may forbid taking an additional staff and sandals for the journey.

Paul applies this principle to the support of ministers (1 Corinthians 9:14; 1 Timothy 5:18).

11.brief: In each town the Twelve are to find out who is worthy and stay there until they leave. They should settle with a receptive household rather than move about seeking better comfort.
11.explain:
“Now whatever city or town you enter, inquire who in it is worthy,”

When they arrive in a town, they are to look for someone “worthy.” This means a person who is open to them and their message, someone willing to receive them.

“and stay there till you go out.”

Once they find such a home, they are to stay there. They are not to move from house to house looking for better lodging.
11.notes: Luke 10:7 adds the command not to go from house to house.

12.brief: When Jesus’ messengers enter a household, they are to greet it. Their arrival opens with a word of blessing.
12.explain:
“And when you go into a household, greet it.”

They are to offer a greeting when they enter. The usual greeting was a blessing of peace (Luke 10:5).
12.notes: The common Hebrew greeting was shalom, a word that means peace and wholeness.

13.brief: If the household is worthy, the messengers’ peace will rest on it, but if not, their peace will return to them. The blessing they offer comes to rest on those who welcome it.
13.explain:
“If the household is worthy, let your peace come upon it.”

If the household welcomes them, the blessing of peace rests on it. The greeting carries God’s blessing.

“But if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you.”

If the household rejects them, the blessing comes back to the messengers. It is not wasted, and they lose nothing.
13.notes: The picture treats the spoken blessing as something real that goes out and either rests on a home or returns.

14.brief: If anyone will not receive Jesus’ messengers or listen to their words, they are to shake the dust off their feet as they leave that house or town. The gesture is a solemn sign that the people have rejected God’s message and its responsibility is now theirs.
14.explain:
“And whoever will not receive you nor hear your words,”

Some will refuse both the messengers and their message.

“when you depart from that house or city, shake off the dust from your feet.”

This gesture was a sign that the people who rejected them were responsible for their choice. The messengers had delivered God’s word, and the responsibility now rested with the hearers.
14.notes: Paul and Barnabas did this when they were driven out of Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51).

15.brief: Jesus solemnly declares that the day of judgment will be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town. To reject the King’s messengers is a greater sin than the notorious wickedness of those ancient cities.
15.explain:
“Assuredly, I say to you,”

Jesus introduces a solemn warning.

“it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city!”

“Sodom and Gomorrah” were destroyed for their wickedness (Genesis 19:24–25). Yet a town that rejects the King’s messengers will face greater judgment. Greater light brings greater accountability. Sodom never heard the message these towns are hearing.
15.notes: Jesus will make the same comparison about Capernaum in 11:23–24.

16.brief: Jesus sends them out “as sheep in the midst of wolves” and tells them to be “wise as serpents and harmless as doves.” Vulnerable among hostile people, they need shrewd discernment joined with innocent integrity.
16.explain:
“Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves.”

Jesus now looks beyond the immediate journey. His messengers will be vulnerable, like “sheep” surrounded by “wolves.” The world will be hostile.

“Therefore be wise as serpents and harmless as doves.”

They need two qualities. They must be “wise as serpents,” shrewd and careful, aware of danger. They must also be “harmless as doves,” innocent and pure, without deceit. Wisdom without innocence becomes cunning. Innocence without wisdom becomes naivety. The disciple needs both.
16.notes: The Greek word translated “harmless” means unmixed or pure. Paul uses it in Romans 16:19, where he wants believers to be wise in what is good and simple concerning evil.

17.brief: Jesus warns them to beware of people who will hand them over to councils and flog them in their synagogues. His messengers will face official opposition, even from religious authorities.
17.explain:
“But beware of men,”

Jesus warns His disciples to be careful. Opposition will come from people.

“for they will deliver you up to councils and scourge you in their synagogues.”

They will be handed over to “councils,” local Jewish courts. They will be whipped in “synagogues,” where such punishments were carried out. The opposition will come first from their own people.
17.notes: Paul received the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes five times (2 Corinthians 11:24). The apostles were beaten by order of the Sanhedrin (Acts 5:40).

18.brief: Jesus’ messengers will be brought before governors and kings for His sake as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles. Jesus’ words now reach beyond this first mission, and their sufferings will become opportunities to bear witness to rulers and nations.
18.explain:
“You will be brought before governors and kings for My sake,”

The persecution will reach higher authorities. They will stand before “governors and kings” because of their loyalty to Jesus.

“as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.”

Even this suffering has a purpose. When they stand trial, they will bear witness to Jesus before rulers “and to the Gentiles.” Here the horizon widens beyond the mission to Israel. The book of Acts shows this happening. Paul testified before the governors Felix and Festus and before King Agrippa (Acts 24–26).
18.notes: Jesus tells Ananias that Paul is a chosen vessel to bear His name before Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel (Acts 9:15).

19.brief: When Jesus’ messengers are handed over for trial, they are not to worry about how or what to speak, because what they should say will be given to them in that hour. The promise meets them at the moment of testimony before their accusers.
19.explain:
“But when they deliver you up, do not worry about how or what you should speak.”

Jesus tells them not to worry ahead of time about what they will say when they are on trial.

“For it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak;”

The right words “will be given” to them when the time comes. This promise does not excuse laziness in learning God’s word. It is a promise for disciples under pressure, standing before authorities because of their faith.
19.notes: The same command not to worry appears in 6:25–34.

20.brief: It is not the messengers themselves who speak, “but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” The Father Himself, through His Spirit, will supply their words in the hour of trial.
20.explain:
“for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

God’s Spirit will be the source of their words. He will speak through them. They will not stand alone.

When Peter and John stood before the council, Peter was filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke boldly. The rulers marveled, because they saw that these were uneducated and untrained men (Acts 4:8–13).
20.notes: Jesus calls God your Father. The Spirit who helps them is the Spirit of the Father who cares for them.

21.brief: Brother will betray brother to death, a father his child, and children will turn against their parents and have them put to death. Allegiance to Jesus can split even the closest families.
21.explain:
“Now brother will deliver up brother to death, and a father his child;”

The opposition will reach into families. Brothers will betray brothers. Fathers will hand over their children.

“and children will rise up against parents and cause them to be put to death.”

Children will turn against parents. Loyalty to Jesus can divide even the closest relationships.
21.notes: These words echo Micah 7:6, which Jesus quotes in 10:35–36.

22.brief: Jesus’ messengers will be hated by all because of His name, “But he who endures to the end will be saved.” Jesus gives a real promise of salvation to the one who endures, and that faithful perseverance through hatred marks those who belong to Him.
22.explain:
“And you will be hated by all for My name’s sake.”

The disciples will be hated “by all.” The reason is “My name’s sake,” their loyalty to Jesus.

“But he who endures to the end will be saved.”

Jesus calls for endurance. Endurance does not earn salvation. It shows the reality of faith in Jesus, the faith that holds on to Him through suffering.

23.brief: When the Twelve are persecuted in one town, they are to flee to another, for they will not finish going through the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes. Jesus’ resurrection in royal authority would come first and open the mission to all nations, while His return in glory remains the final horizon for a mission to Israel that is not yet finished.
23.explain:
“When they persecute you in this city, flee to another.”

Jesus gives permission to flee. When persecution comes in one place, they may go to another. Fleeing danger is not cowardice. It allows the message to spread to new places. The church in Acts was scattered by persecution and preached wherever it went (Acts 8:1, 4).

“For assuredly, I say to you, you will not have gone through the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes.”

Jesus promises that He will come before they have finished going through Israel’s towns. Their mission is urgent, and it will not be completed before He comes.

This coming has a decisive first stage in Jesus’ resurrection. When He rose, He received all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18). That authority opened the mission beyond Israel to all nations (28:19), before the disciples had finished Israel’s towns. The final horizon is Jesus’ return in glory. The mission to Israel continues until then.
23.notes: This verse has been understood in many ways. Jesus’ resurrection authority (28:18–20) and His final return in glory (25:31) belong together in its horizon.

24.brief: A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. Those who follow Jesus must expect to share His treatment.
24.explain:
“A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master.”

Jesus states a general principle. A student does not rank above his teacher. A servant does not rank above his master. Disciples should expect to be treated as Jesus is treated.
24.notes: Jesus uses the same saying in John 13:16 and 15:20. In John 15:20 He adds, “If they persecuted Me, they will also persecute you.”

25.brief: It is enough for a disciple to be like his teacher, and if they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, they will call His household worse. If Jesus’ enemies slander Him as satanic, His followers cannot expect better treatment.
25.explain:
“It is enough for a disciple that he be like his teacher, and a servant like his master.”

The goal of a disciple is to become like his teacher. That is enough. It includes sharing in His treatment by the world.

“If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more will they call those of his household!”

Jesus Himself has been accused of working by the power of the ruler of demons (9:34). The Pharisees call Him “Beelzebub,” a name for Satan. If they insult the head of the household this way, His disciples should expect the same.
25.notes: Beelzebub may come from Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2), whose name means lord of flies. The form Beelzebul may mean lord of the dwelling.

26.brief: Therefore they are not to fear their opponents, for nothing covered will remain hidden. God will bring the truth to light, so slander and secrecy will not have the last word.
26.explain:
“Therefore do not fear them.”

Jesus tells His disciples not to be afraid of their persecutors. This command appears three times in this section (10:26, 28, 31).

“For there is nothing covered that will not be revealed, and hidden that will not be known.”

The truth will come out. Whatever is now hidden will be revealed. The slanders against Jesus and His disciples will be exposed, and God will make the truth known.
26.notes: Luke 12:2–3 applies this saying to the hypocrisy of the Pharisees.

27.brief: What Jesus tells them in the dark they are to speak in the light, and what they hear privately they are to proclaim from the housetops. The message He entrusts to them must be declared boldly and publicly.
27.explain:
“Whatever I tell you in the dark, speak in the light;”

What Jesus teaches His disciples privately, they are to proclaim openly.

“and what you hear in the ear, preach on the housetops.”

Flat roofs were a public place in Israelite towns. What they heard whispered, they are to proclaim from the rooftops for everyone to hear. The gospel is not a secret to be kept.
27.notes: Announcements were sometimes made from rooftops, where a voice could carry across a town.

28.brief: They are not to fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul, but rather to fear Him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Reverent fear of God, the Judge of all, frees disciples from the fear of people.
28.explain:
“And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.”

The persecutors can only harm the body. They can kill, but their power ends there. They cannot touch the soul.

“But rather fear Him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.”

The One to fear is God. He alone has authority over both “soul and body.” He is the Judge of all. This is not Satan. Reverent fear of God frees the disciple from the fear of people.
28.notes: The Greek word translated “hell” is Gehenna, a valley south of Jerusalem associated with idolatry and burning. It became a name for the place of final judgment.

29.brief: Two sparrows sell for a copper coin, yet not one falls to the ground apart from the Father’s will. The Father’s care reaches even the cheapest of His creatures.
29.explain:
“Are not two sparrows sold for a copper coin?”

Jesus turns from the fear of God to the Father’s care. “Sparrows” were among the cheapest things sold in the market. Two could be bought for one small coin.

“And not one of them falls to the ground apart from your Father’s will.”

Yet God sees every sparrow. Not one dies without His knowledge and will. If God cares for something so small, He cares much more for His children.
29.notes: The Greek text reads literally apart from your Father. The NKJV adds will to clarify the sense. Luke 12:6 says that not one of them is forgotten before God.

30.brief: Even the hairs of their heads are all numbered. The Father knows and cares for His children down to the smallest detail.
30.explain:
“But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.”

God knows every detail of His children’s lives. He knows the number of hairs on their heads. Nothing about them is too small for His attention.
30.notes: The same idea appears in Luke 21:18, where Jesus says that not a hair of their head shall be lost.

31.brief: So they are not to fear, because they are worth more than many sparrows. The Father’s detailed care gives His children courage in the face of danger.
31.explain:
“Do not fear therefore;”

Because of the Father’s care, the disciples need not be afraid.

“you are of more value than many sparrows.”

They are worth far more to God than birds. If He watches over sparrows, He will watch over them. This does not mean they will never suffer. Jesus has just told them they may be killed (10:28). It means that nothing happens to them outside the Father’s care.
31.notes: Jesus uses a similar argument about the birds of the air in 6:26.

32.brief: Whoever confesses Jesus before people, He will confess before His Father in heaven. Those who publicly own their allegiance to Jesus will be owned by Him before the Father.
32.explain:
“Therefore whoever confesses Me before men,”

To confess Jesus is to openly acknowledge Him as Lord, even when it is costly.

“him I will also confess before My Father who is in heaven.”

Jesus promises that He will acknowledge such a person before His Father. In the final judgment, Jesus will speak for those who spoke for Him.
32.notes: Romans 10:9 links confession with salvation: “if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, you will be saved.”

33.brief: But whoever denies Him before people, He will deny before His Father. The stakes of public allegiance to Jesus are eternal.
33.explain:
“But whoever denies Me before men, him I will also deny before My Father who is in heaven.”

The warning is serious. Those who deny Jesus will be denied by Him before the Father.

Peter later denied Jesus three times (26:69–75). Yet he wept bitterly, and Jesus restored him (John 21:15–19). The warning concerns a settled refusal to acknowledge Jesus, not a failure that is followed by repentance.
33.notes: Paul writes, “If we deny Him, He also will deny us” (2 Timothy 2:12).

34.brief: Jesus tells them not to think He came to bring peace on earth: “I did not come to bring peace but a sword.” His coming forces a decision that divides people according to how they respond to Him.
34.explain:
“Do not think that I came to bring peace on earth.”

Jesus corrects a false expectation. Some might think the Messiah would bring immediate peace to everyone.

“I did not come to bring peace but a sword.”

Jesus brings peace with God to those who receive Him. But His coming also divides. The “sword” pictures division, not violence by His followers. People respond to Him in different ways, and that response divides even families.
34.notes: Luke 12:51 records the same saying with the word division in place of sword.

35.brief: He has come to set a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. Echoing Micah 7:6, Jesus warns that loyalty to Him can divide even households.
35.explain:
“For I have come to ‘set a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law’;”

Jesus quotes Micah 7:6. The division will reach into households. When one family member follows Jesus and another does not, the closest relationships can be torn.
35.notes: In Micah 7:6 these words describe the breakdown of trust in a corrupt society. Jesus applies them to the division His coming brings.

36.brief: A man’s enemies will be the members of his own household. The opposition a disciple faces may come from those closest to him.
36.explain:
“and ‘a man’s enemies will be those of his own household.”

The quotation continues. The people who oppose a disciple may be in his own home. Loyalty to Jesus can cost the approval of one’s own family.
36.notes: Micah 7:7 continues, “Therefore I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation.”

37.brief: Whoever loves father or mother, son or daughter, more than Jesus is not worthy of Him. Jesus claims a love that ranks above the deepest human loyalties.
37.explain:
“He who loves father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me.”

Jesus claims first place in His disciples’ love. Love for parents is good and commanded by God (15:4). But no one may love even father or mother more than Jesus. Only God can rightly make such a claim.

“And he who loves son or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me.”

The same is true of children. Even the love of a parent for a child must not come before love for Jesus.
37.notes: Luke 14:26 uses stronger language: if anyone comes to Jesus and does not hate his father and mother, he cannot be His disciple. In Hebrew idiom, to hate can mean to love less.

38.brief: Whoever does not take up his cross and follow Jesus is not worthy of Him. Following Him means yielding self-rule and staying faithful even when obedience costs suffering or death.
38.explain:
“And he who does not take his cross and follow after Me is not worthy of Me.”

This is the first mention of the cross in Matthew. A condemned person carried his own cross to the place of execution. To “take his cross” means to give up control of one’s own life and follow Jesus, even if it costs one’s life.

Jesus’ own death on the cross remains unique. Only His death pays for sin. A disciple’s cross is faithful obedience to Him, whatever it costs.

39.brief: Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for Jesus’ sake will find it. Clinging to self ends in loss, while giving oneself up for Jesus leads to true life.
39.explain:
“He who finds his life will lose it,”

The person who tries to secure his own life by holding on to it will lose it in the end.

“and he who loses his life for My sake will find it.”

The one who gives up his life “for My sake” will find true life. The key words are “for My sake.” It is loyalty to Jesus that turns loss into gain.
39.notes: The Greek word translated “life” can also mean soul or self.

40.brief: Whoever receives the disciples receives Jesus, and whoever receives Jesus receives the Father who sent Him. Jesus so identifies with His messengers that welcoming them is welcoming Him and His Father.
40.explain:
“He who receives you receives Me,”

Jesus closes with a promise. Those who welcome His messengers welcome Him. The disciples represent Jesus.

“and he who receives Me receives Him who sent Me.”

To receive Jesus is to receive the Father who sent Him. Welcoming a messenger of Jesus is welcoming God Himself.

41.brief: Whoever receives a prophet as a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever receives a righteous man as righteous will receive a righteous man’s reward. Those who welcome God’s servants share in the reward of the servants they support.
41.explain:
“He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward.”

To receive someone this way means to welcome him because he is a prophet. The one who welcomes him shares in the prophet’s reward.

“And he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward.”

The same is true for a “righteous man.” Those who support God’s servants share in their reward.
41.notes: John writes that those who support traveling workers for the truth become fellow workers with them (3 John 5–8).

42.brief: Whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because he is a disciple will by no means lose his reward. The smallest kindness to Jesus’ vulnerable messengers is noticed and rewarded by the King.
42.explain:
“And whoever gives one of these little ones only a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple,”

Even the smallest act of kindness matters. “These little ones” are Jesus’ disciples, His humble messengers. A “cup of cold water” given to one of them because he is a disciple is seen by the King.

“assuredly, I say to you, he shall by no means lose his reward.”

God will not forget such kindness. Jesus will speak of the same principle in 25:40: whatever is done for the least of His brethren is done for Him.
42.notes: The phrase in the name of a disciple means because he is a disciple.
